modalities.name: Inner Roster Games
modalities.tagline: Rotate team roles and meet the inner parts that push back.
modalities.whatItIs: Inner Roster Games is a new, untested concept halfway between recreational team sport and Internal Family Systems, a form of parts work that sees the mind as a family of inner parts. A small group plays relaxed, non-contact games while deliberately rotating through roles such as leading, defending or sitting a round out, then pauses to notice which part reacts to each one.
modalities.coreIdea: Most of us fall into the same role on any team, and the parts that guard it, such as the one that must win or the one that hides, show up most clearly when we try a different role. Meeting those parts with curiosity in the middle of play, rather than in a therapy room, may make them easier to recognize in everyday life.
modalities.whatYouDo: Eight to twelve people meet in a park for 90 minutes with a facilitator trained in group work and play short rounds of a slow-paced disc or ball game at walking or jogging pace. Before each round everyone takes a role they rarely choose, and afterwards the group huddles for two minutes so each player can name the part that showed up, for example 'a part of me wanted to disappear', without anyone analyzing it. The session ends in a circle where players share what it was like to play from a calmer, more curious place.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who learn better by doing than by talking, and who notice they always end up as the leader, the helper or the one on the sidelines and want to understand what that habit protects.
modalities.cautions: Running and catching bring a risk of sprains and knocks, so warm up, keep the game non-contact and check with a doctor first if you have heart or joint problems. Old feelings about being picked last or judged can surface, so sharing is always optional, and anyone with severe trauma or in crisis should work with a licensed therapist rather than rely on a game.
modalities.tweet: New concept: Inner Roster Games. A relaxed team game where you swap into roles you usually avoid, then huddle to notice which part of you pushed back. For anyone who always ends up the leader, the helper or the one on the sidelines and wonders why.

modalities.name: The Pacing Council
modalities.tagline: An easy run where your inner voices negotiate the pace.
modalities.whatItIs: The Pacing Council is a proposed practice halfway between Internal Family Systems, which sees inner voices as parts with their own intentions, and steady endurance exercise such as running. During an easy run or brisk walk, the voice that pushes you faster and the voice that wants to stop are each heard as a part with its own worries, in time with your steps.
modalities.coreIdea: Steady effort over half an hour or more reliably brings out the same inner pushers and quitters, one after another, which makes a run a natural meeting place for them. The aim is to obey neither but to hear what each one fears, and then let a calmer, more curious part of you set the pace.
modalities.whatYouDo: Two or three times a week you go out alone for 30 to 45 minutes at a pace where you could still talk, after a few first outings alongside a coach or guide trained in parts work. When a strong voice shows up, such as 'you are too slow' or 'just stop', you ease off slightly and silently ask what it is afraid would happen, letting an answer come in rhythm with your footsteps. Afterwards you spend five minutes noting which voices came, when, and what they seemed to want.
modalities.whoItsFor: Runners and walkers who hear a harsh inner coach or a voice that always wants to quit, and people who think more clearly on the move than sitting across from someone.
modalities.cautions: Pain, chest discomfort, dizziness or unusual breathlessness are signals to stop, not voices to negotiate with, and anyone with heart or other medical conditions should get medical advice first and build up gradually. If old, painful memories come up strongly, slow to a walk and take them to a trained therapist, since this untested idea is not a substitute for trauma care.
modalities.tweet: An idea for runners: The Pacing Council. On an easy run, the voice that pushes you and the voice that wants to quit become parts with their own fears. Hear each one out, then let your calmer self choose the pace. For anyone with a harsh inner coach.

modalities.name: Burden and Barbell
modalities.tagline: Lift a real weight, set it down, and notice what you carry.
modalities.whatItIs: Burden and Barbell is a new concept that blends an idea from Internal Family Systems, that inner parts can carry burdens of old beliefs and feelings, with the set structure of strength training. Each set pairs a moderate physical load with one inner load you name beforehand, and slowly putting the weight down becomes a felt rehearsal of choosing what you keep carrying.
modalities.coreIdea: A weight you can feel in your hands makes the idea of carrying something heavy concrete, and so does the relief of setting it down. Practicing that contrast inside a predictable routine gives protective parts a safe, bodily taste of putting a load down, without forcing a dive into where the burden came from.
modalities.whatYouDo: Once a week you meet a strength coach with training in parts work for a 40-minute session of carries, squats and presses at loads that feel moderately hard, in sets of 8 to 12. Before each set you name one thing a part of you feels it must hold up, such as 'keeping everyone happy', then lift or carry the weight with full attention and set it down slowly, noticing what changes in your hands, shoulders and breath. Between sets you rest, breathe and write one line about what letting go felt like.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who feel they have to hold everything together, and who find it easier to feel a change in the body than to talk one through.
modalities.cautions: Use moderate loads with good technique, breathe out on the effort instead of holding your breath, and get medical advice first if you have high blood pressure or heart or eye problems. Strong emotions can arrive mid-set, so pause whenever you need to, and keep deep trauma work with a licensed therapist, as this untested idea is a complement to care, not a replacement.
modalities.tweet: Untested idea: Burden and Barbell. Name something you feel you must hold up, lift or carry a moderate weight, then set it down slowly and notice the relief. A strength session for people who always feel they have to hold everything together.

modalities.name: Brush and Befriend
modalities.tagline: Groom a calm animal and practice the care a young part needs.
modalities.whatItIs: Brush and Befriend is a proposed, therapist-led practice halfway between Internal Family Systems, which sees the mind as made of many inner parts, and animal-assisted therapy. You spend unhurried time grooming a calm, trained dog or horse, and the slow, patient touch the animal responds to becomes a model for approaching the young, hurt parts of yourself.
modalities.coreIdea: An animal will not accept being rushed or forced, so caring for one teaches, through your hands, the gentle and patient attention that hurt inner parts also seem to need. Once you have felt what that kind of care is like on the outside, it may be easier to offer it on the inside.
modalities.whatYouDo: In a weekly 60-minute session at a farm or clinic, a licensed therapist and a trained animal team guide you as you brush, stroke or simply sit with a calm animal. The therapist helps you notice which part shows up as you approach, such as an impatient one or one that expects rejection, and later invites you to picture offering the same patient touch to a part of you that feels small or scared. The session closes with a few quiet minutes beside the animal and a short talk about what you noticed.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who are far kinder to animals than to themselves, and people who find it easier to open up with an animal in the room than face to face with a therapist.
modalities.cautions: Allergies, fear of animals, bites, scratches and, around horses, kicks and falls are real risks, so contact is always voluntary and supervised, hygiene rules apply, and the animal gets rest breaks and is free to walk away. Turning toward hurt parts can bring up painful memories, so this untested concept belongs with a licensed clinician and is not suited to a current crisis.
modalities.tweet: What if brushing a calm horse could teach you to be gentle with the hurt parts of yourself? Brush and Befriend is a new idea: slow, patient grooming with a therapist nearby, for people who are far kinder to animals than to themselves.

modalities.name: Step-Back Sequence
modalities.tagline: Open outward to give a feeling space, then return to center.
modalities.whatItIs: Step-Back Sequence is a new concept that joins the slow, breath-paced movements of qigong to unblending, a skill from Internal Family Systems that means stepping back from a feeling or inner part just enough to see it. A short set form alternates movements that open away from the body with movements that return to the center, giving that inner step back a physical shape.
modalities.coreIdea: Stepping back from a part is hard to grasp in words but easy to feel in the arms: as you open outward on the out-breath you leave a little room between you and the part, and as you return you check how you now feel toward it. Repeating the same calm form each day gives you a steady home base for meeting parts.
modalities.whatYouDo: You learn the form in a small class or one to one with a qigong teacher who has trauma-informed training, then practice it for about 20 minutes, standing or seated. After a few minutes of easy loosening, you bring to mind a part that is active today, such as a worried or irritated one, and do eight slow rounds of opening and returning with the breath, asking on each return whether you feel a little more curious or calm toward it. You finish with a minute of still standing and a few lines in a notebook.
modalities.whoItsFor: People drawn to parts work who get lost or flooded when they sit still and look inward, and people who would rather meet their feelings while moving gently.
modalities.cautions: The movements are gentle, but sit or adapt them if standing makes you dizzy or sore, and anyone with a history of psychosis or another serious mental illness should get medical advice and an experienced teacher before starting qigong. When practicing alone, work with everyday parts rather than deep trauma, which belongs with a licensed therapist; this is an untested idea.
modalities.tweet: Concept: Step-Back Sequence. A short qigong-style routine where each slow outward movement puts some room between you and a worried or angry part of you, and each return checks how you feel toward it. For people who can't sit still with their feelings.

modalities.name: Plus-Ones Evening
modalities.tagline: A gathering where friends introduce the inner parts they bring along.
modalities.whatItIs: Plus-Ones Evening is a proposed social practice halfway between Internal Family Systems, which pictures the mind as a family of inner parts, and regular socializing. Friends or members of a small club meet over food, and each introduces one of the parts that comes along to their social life, such as the joker, the worrier or the people-pleaser, as if it were a plus-one.
modalities.coreIdea: When the people around you know your protective parts by name, a sharp remark or a sudden silence can be met with curiosity instead of being taken personally. Naming parts together, lightly and with warmth, turns an inner idea into a shared language for friendship.
modalities.whatYouDo: Once a month, four to eight people gather for a two-hour meal with a host who has some training in group facilitation and keeps the tone light. Partway through, each person introduces one part that often shows up around others, for example 'my rescuer, who jumps in whenever anyone is upset', and what it might be protecting, and the others simply thank it rather than analyze it. Before leaving, everyone agrees on a friendly phrase to use when they spot that part in each other during the month.
modalities.whoItsFor: Friends, housemates or club members who want to understand each other's reactions better, and people who feel they turn into someone else in company and want to explore why.
modalities.cautions: This is a social gathering, not group therapy: nobody has to share, what is said stays in the room, and anyone with intense social fear, lasting low mood or a current crisis should talk to a doctor or therapist. Keep the focus on everyday parts, since deep or traumatic material needs a trained clinician, and remember the concept itself is untested.
modalities.tweet: Dinner-party concept: Plus-Ones Evening. Each guest introduces one inner part they bring to social life, like the joker or the worrier, and what it protects. A shared language so friends can stop taking each other's reactions personally.

modalities.name: Field Guide to Parts
modalities.tagline: On a slow walk, let the landscape show you your parts.
modalities.whatItIs: Field Guide to Parts is an untested concept halfway between Internal Family Systems, a form of parts work, and nature walks. On a slow, open-ended walk you notice what in the landscape catches your eye, such as a twisted tree, a guarded nest or a fast stream, and let it stand for one of your inner parts, building a personal field guide over time.
modalities.coreIdea: Parts are often easier to meet when they first appear outside you, and nature offers endless living images to see them in, with no pressure to perform. Sitting beside a weathered stump that reminds you of a tired protector lets you get curious about that part in a soft, unhurried way.
modalities.whatYouDo: You walk for 60 to 90 minutes in a quiet park, woodland or coastline with the phone away and no set route, at first with a guide trained in parts work and later alone or with a friend. When something draws your attention, you stop, ask which part of you it brings to mind, and spend a few minutes near it, noticing how you feel toward that part. At home you add a sketch, photo or note to your field guide, such as 'the heron: the part of me that waits and watches'.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who feel more at ease outdoors than in a therapy room, and people curious about their inner parts who find images easier to work with than direct questions.
modalities.cautions: Plan the route, check the weather, carry water and tell someone where you are going, since slips, heat, cold and getting lost are real outdoor risks. Strong feelings can surface on a quiet walk, so keep deep or traumatic material for sessions with a trained therapist and use this as a complement to care, not a replacement.
modalities.tweet: Thought experiment: could a woodland walk help you meet the different parts of yourself? Field Guide to Parts: notice what catches your eye, a twisted tree, a fast stream, and ask which part of you it brings to mind. For people who think better outdoors.

modalities.name: Clear Window Sitting
modalities.tagline: Your senses as a gauge of how caught up you are.
modalities.whatItIs: Clear Window Sitting is a new concept for a seated practice halfway between Internal Family Systems, a form of parts work, and sensory mindfulness. It uses the plain senses, what you see, hear and feel against the chair, as a gauge of how far an inner part such as worry or anger has taken over your view.
modalities.coreIdea: When a part takes charge, the senses can shift with it: sounds may seem sharper, the visual field narrower, the room less vivid. Noticing how the window of perception clears as the part steps back gives you a concrete, present-moment sign that you are less caught up in it.
modalities.whatYouDo: After learning it with a teacher or guide, you sit alone for about 20 minutes in a quiet room. You spend two or three minutes simply looking and listening, then bring to mind a mild, current worry and notice how colors, sounds and the feel of the chair change as the worried part comes forward. You then kindly ask that part to step back a little, look and listen again, and repeat the round two or three times, noting what clears.
modalities.whoItsFor: People drawn to parts work who find it hard to tell from the inside whether a feeling has taken over, and people who prefer concrete sensory anchors to abstract inner work.
modalities.cautions: Use mild, present-day concerns rather than painful memories, and if something strong comes up, open your eyes, feel your feet on the floor and stop. Meditation-style practice can occasionally bring up difficult experiences, so people with a history of trauma, dissociation or psychosis should work with a trained therapist; the idea is untested.
modalities.tweet: Does the room get louder when you're anxious? Clear Window Sitting, an experimental practice: look and listen, bring up a small worry, notice how sounds and colors change, then ask the worry to step back. A way to sense when a feeling has taken over.

modalities.name: Every Part Plays
modalities.tagline: Give each inner part its own instrument and listen to the ensemble.
modalities.whatItIs: Every Part Plays is a proposed practice halfway between Internal Family Systems, a therapy built around inner parts, and music therapy. With a music therapist, you give each of your parts its own sound on simple instruments, such as a pounding drum for an angry protector or a soft chime for a shy young part, and then let them play together while you listen.
modalities.coreIdea: Some parts have no words, but almost any part can make a sound, and hearing parts play side by side shows how they relate: who drowns out whom, and who never gets a turn. Listening to the whole ensemble from a calm, curious place is a musical way of leading your inner life instead of being run by one part.
modalities.whatYouDo: In a weekly 50-minute session with a credentialed music therapist who knows parts work, you choose a drum, shaker, xylophone or your own voice for two or three parts you already know. You play each part's sound in turn, then the therapist helps you play them together, or plays back a recording of all of them, while you step back, listen and talk about which sound wanted more room. Keeping the recordings from week to week lets you hear how the ensemble changes.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who find it hard to put feelings into words, whether or not they are musical, and people in parts work who want a more expressive, less talk-based way to hear from their parts.
modalities.cautions: Music can stir strong emotions and old memories, so this untested idea belongs with a credentialed music therapist, and with a licensed clinician for any trauma work; it is not suited to a current crisis. Keep the volume moderate to protect your hearing.
modalities.tweet: Imagine giving each part of you an instrument: a loud drum for the angry protector, a soft chime for the shy one. Every Part Plays is a speculative practice where you hear them play together. For people who say more with music than with words.

modalities.name: Check or Carry
modalities.tagline: Sort each sticky thought: test it, or carry it lightly.
modalities.whatItIs: Check or Carry is a new, structured concept halfway between cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT), which tests and changes unhelpful thoughts, and acceptance and commitment therapy (ACT), which teaches you to hold them lightly. Instead of using one approach for every thought, you learn to sort each troubling thought into one of two trays: thoughts worth checking against evidence, and thoughts better carried lightly while you get on with what matters.
modalities.coreIdea: Some thoughts are testable predictions that a small experiment can settle, while others are old, sticky stories that arguing with only feeds. The skill at the heart of this method is telling the two apart, so effort goes where it can pay off and acceptance goes where struggle only makes things worse.
modalities.whatYouDo: Over about eight weekly sessions with a therapist, plus a five-minute daily worksheet, you write down one troubling thought and ask two questions: could I test this in the coming week, and has arguing with it ever helped? Checkable thoughts get a small real-life experiment, while thoughts you have argued with a hundred times get a lighter move, such as saying 'I am having the thought that...' and then taking one step you value anyway. Each week you review how the sorting went and adjust it.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who have tried challenging their thoughts and found that some just bounce back, or who have tried acceptance and wished for something more practical.
modalities.cautions: Generally low risk, though it means regular homework, and the sorting itself can turn into a new way of avoiding hard feelings, which a therapist can help you spot. Severe depression, suicidal thoughts or another serious condition need prompt help from a qualified clinician, and this combined method is untested.
modalities.tweet: Not every anxious thought deserves a debate. Check or Carry is a new concept: sort each sticky thought into 'test it this week' or 'carry it lightly and act anyway'. For anyone whose worst thoughts bounce back however hard they argue.

modalities.name: Hidden Rule Experiments
modalities.tagline: Find the emotional rule behind a habit, then test it live.
modalities.whatItIs: Hidden Rule Experiments is a proposed, therapist-led method halfway between cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) and Coherence Therapy. It assumes that a stubborn habit, such as putting things off or people-pleasing, often obeys an unspoken emotional rule learned long ago, and it pairs uncovering that rule with real-life experiments designed to show the rule is wrong.
modalities.coreIdea: CBT tests thoughts against evidence, while Coherence Therapy holds that a symptom stops being needed when the emotional learning behind it meets a vivid contradiction. Here the experiments aim not at surface thoughts but at the hidden rule itself, so you feel the old rule and its contradiction at the same time.
modalities.whatYouDo: Over 8 to 12 weekly sessions with a licensed therapist, you start with structured sentence completions such as 'If I stopped putting things off, I would have to feel...' to bring the hidden rule into words. Together you then design one small experiment a week in which the rule's prediction can visibly fail, for example asking for help when the rule says people leave if you need them, and you go in holding the old rule consciously in mind. Later sessions check whether the old reaction still fires in situations that used to set it off.
modalities.whoItsFor: People with a specific pattern that keeps returning despite good coping skills, who want to understand why it happens and prefer structured, practical steps to open-ended talk.
modalities.cautions: Uncovering an old emotional rule can be intense, so people with severe trauma, dissociation or a current crisis should do this only with a licensed clinician experienced in trauma, and possible medical causes of a symptom need ruling out first. It is an untested combination and should not replace well-tested care for conditions such as major depression or PTSD.
modalities.tweet: Your stubborn habit may obey an old emotional rule, like 'if I ask for help, people leave'. Hidden Rule Experiments, a proposed method: name the rule with a therapist, then run small real-life tests where it can fail. For patterns that outlast every tip.

modalities.name: Dimmer Switch Shaking
modalities.tagline: Graded, stoppable shaking to build trust in letting go.
modalities.whatItIs: Dimmer Switch Shaking is a new concept that combines the step-by-step structure of cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) with tension and trauma releasing exercises (TRE), in which tired leg muscles begin to tremble on their own. You learn to turn that natural shaking up, down and off at will, in graded steps, while tracking how confident you feel about letting go and staying in charge.
modalities.coreIdea: Many tense, anxious people fear that if they loosen their grip on the body, something will spin out of control. Practicing a reflex you can dim and stop at any moment, in small planned steps, tests that fear directly and is meant to show that you can let go and still be in charge.
modalities.whatYouDo: Over six weekly 45-minute sessions with a provider trained in both approaches, followed by home practice, you first write down what you predict will happen if you let the shaking run and rate your sense of control from 0 to 10. You then do a short, set sequence of leg-tiring exercises and lie down for a planned stretch of tremoring, starting with a minute or two, practicing turning it down by shifting your legs and stopping it by straightening them. Afterwards you re-rate your sense of control, compare it with your prediction, and add a minute only when the last step felt manageable.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who carry a lot of tension but feel uneasy about losing control of their body, especially those who like clear steps and measurable progress.
modalities.cautions: Strong emotions or memories can surface, so people with severe trauma, dissociation, psychosis, bipolar disorder or another serious condition should learn tremor work only with a clinically trained provider, alongside their own care. Check with a doctor first if you have epilepsy or seizures, are pregnant, or have recent surgery or injuries, and stop whenever you feel overwhelmed, dizzy or in pain; the idea is untested.
modalities.tweet: Tense, but afraid to let go? Dimmer Switch Shaking, an invented practice: gentle tremor exercises in small planned steps, where you learn to turn the body's natural shaking up, down and off, and test the fear that letting go means losing control.

modalities.name: The Landing Column
modalities.tagline: A balanced thought must fit the facts and feel right inside.
modalities.whatItIs: The Landing Column is a proposed journaling method halfway between cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) and Focusing. It takes the familiar CBT thought record, where you weigh an upsetting thought against the evidence and write a more balanced one, and adds a final column that asks whether the new thought actually lands in the body.
modalities.coreIdea: A balanced thought that makes sense on paper often fails to feel true, and the 'felt sense' of Focusing, a vague bodily sense of a situation before it is in words, can tell you what is missing. Rewording until the thought both fits the evidence and brings a small felt 'yes' joins logical checking with bodily checking.
modalities.whatYouDo: You learn the method in a few sessions with a therapist or Focusing-trained coach, then use it alone for about 20 minutes when something upsets you. After writing the situation, the upsetting thought, the evidence and a more balanced alternative, you pause with eyes closed and sense whether the new thought lands, and if it does not, you ask that felt sense what is missing. You rewrite and check again until there is a small sense of relief or fit, then note it in the last column.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who say 'I know it is not true, but it still feels true', and people who like structured tools but want them to reach beyond the head.
modalities.cautions: Usually gentle, but turning inward can bring up strong feelings or memories, and the bodily check should never be used to force yourself into agreeing with a thought. Severe depression, trauma or a current crisis call for a qualified therapist rather than self-help, and this method is untested.
modalities.tweet: Ever written a 'balanced thought' that still felt false? The Landing Column, a new idea: add one last step to your thought journal, close your eyes, and check whether the new thought lands in your body. Keep rewording until something inside says yes.

modalities.name: Living Agenda Coaching
modalities.tagline: Coaching plans that grow from what is already alive in you.
modalities.whatItIs: Living Agenda Coaching is a new concept for one-to-one coaching halfway between cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) and Aletheia Coaching, a slow, presence-based style that helps what a person already feels come into awareness. Each session joins an unhurried, feeling-led check-in, in which the coach reflects back not only your words but how you say them, with a clear agenda and one practical step to try before the next meeting.
modalities.coreIdea: Like an acorn that already holds an oak, the next step grows from what feels alive and wanted in you right now, not from a list of what is wrong with you. A simple plan and checkable steps keep that unfolding grounded, so depth and practical progress work together.
modalities.whatYouDo: Every two weeks for about three months you meet a coach trained in both styles for 60 minutes. For the first 15 minutes you speak from what you feel rather than about it while the coach notices tone, pauses and posture, and then together you set one agenda item and design a small real-world step for the next two weeks. The next session reviews both what happened and how it felt, and the plan grows from there.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who are not in crisis and want personal growth that is both deep and practical, for example those who find goal-setting coaching too shallow and open-ended inner work too vague.
modalities.cautions: This is coaching, not therapy, so the coach must be able to recognize trauma and refer on, and anyone with severe depression, PTSD, suicidal thoughts or another serious condition should work with a qualified mental health professional. Strong feelings can come up when you slow down, so go at your own pace; the approach is untested.
modalities.tweet: Proposed: Living Agenda Coaching. Each session starts slow, with you speaking from what you feel, then turns that into one concrete step for the next two weeks. Growth plans that start from what is already alive in you, not from what is wrong with you.

modalities.name: The Empty Appointment
modalities.tagline: Schedule doing nothing, protect it, and answer the thoughts that cancel it.
modalities.whatItIs: The Empty Appointment is a proposed practice halfway between the planning tools of cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) and Do Nothing meditation, a style of sitting whose only instruction is to let whatever happens happen. You book short sessions of doing nothing at all into your calendar like any other commitment, and use simple CBT steps to notice and answer the thoughts that try to cancel them.
modalities.coreIdea: Many busy, self-critical people see rest as something they have to earn, so it rarely happens. Making non-doing a planned, protected appointment, and looking honestly at the thoughts that call it lazy or pointless, aims to turn letting go into a habit rather than a reward.
modalities.whatYouDo: After learning the basics from a book, app or teacher, you keep a 15-minute appointment most days, sit somewhere comfortable and drop any effort to plan, solve or improve anything, letting the mind wander as it likes. Beforehand you jot down any thought that argues against it, such as 'this is a waste of time', and afterwards you rate how the appointment actually went and how the rest of the day felt. Once a week you look back at the log and notice which cancelling thoughts turned out to be true.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who cannot stop working on themselves, who feel guilty when they rest, or who find standard meditation instructions just another task to get right.
modalities.cautions: With nothing to focus on, some people drift into worry or doze off, and like any meditation, open sitting can occasionally bring up difficult feelings or memories. It is an untested self-care idea, not a form of therapy, so persistent low mood or anxiety calls for a doctor or therapist.
modalities.tweet: Rest shouldn't be a reward you have to earn. The Empty Appointment is a new concept: 15 minutes in your calendar for doing nothing at all, plus a quick note of the thoughts that try to cancel it. For people who feel guilty resting.

modalities.name: Well-Wishing Ladder
modalities.tagline: Build goodwill step by step, from the easiest person upward.
modalities.whatItIs: Well-Wishing Ladder is a new concept that crosses the graded steps of exposure work in cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) with loving-kindness (metta) meditation, the practice of silently wishing people well. You rank people from easiest to hardest to wish well, rate how hard each feels, and climb the ladder one rung at a time.
modalities.coreIdea: Exposure work builds tolerance by facing fears in small, manageable steps, and the same logic may apply to goodwill. Starting where kindness comes easily and moving up only when a rung feels manageable lets the warm feeling grow, while the thoughts that block it are noticed and weighed rather than ignored.
modalities.whatYouDo: Over eight weeks you sit for 15 minutes a day and check in weekly with a meditation teacher or therapist. You list about ten people, from a friend who is easy to love to someone who irritates you, place yourself wherever you honestly fit, and rate each rung from 0 to 10 for difficulty, leaving anyone who has seriously harmed you off the list. Each sitting you repeat phrases such as 'may you be well' toward the current rung until its rating drops, and when a blocking thought appears, such as 'they do not deserve it', you note it, weigh it briefly and return to the phrases.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who want more warmth toward others and themselves but find loving-kindness practice vague or overwhelming, and who like clear steps and visible progress.
modalities.cautions: Wishing people well can stir grief, anger or a sense of unworthiness, especially after trauma or with harsh self-criticism, so start with someone easy, keep sittings short and leave anyone who harmed you off the ladder. People with a history of trauma, psychosis or mania should talk to a clinician first, as this structured approach is untested.
modalities.tweet: Loving-kindness meditation, built like a ladder. Well-Wishing Ladder, a hypothetical practice: rank people from easiest to hardest to wish well and climb one rung at a time, moving up only when ready. For anyone who finds kindness practice too vague.

modalities.name: Thought Pattern Tally
modalities.tagline: Label each thought's type as it passes, then count the visits.
modalities.whatItIs: Thought Pattern Tally is a proposed sitting practice halfway between cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) and vipassana, or insight, meditation. While watching the breath and body, you give each passing thought a one-word label for its type, such as predicting, judging or replaying, and keep a simple tally, so over the weeks you can see which mental habits visit most and how they come and go.
modalities.coreIdea: CBT names common thinking patterns, and insight meditation trains you to watch every experience arise and pass. Labeling thoughts by pattern in real time, without arguing with them, shows both how often a habit appears and that each visit ends on its own.
modalities.whatYouDo: You learn the method in a six-week course with a weekly class, then sit alone for 20 minutes a day. Each time a thought appears, you silently note its type in one word and press a hand counter or make a mark, then return to the breath. After each sitting you write down the tallies and one example, and once a week you look for patterns, such as predicting that spikes on Sunday nights.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who like data and structure and want to understand their own minds, and meditators who want a clearer bridge between what they notice on the cushion and daily life.
modalities.cautions: Seeing how often worry shows up can be unsettling at first, and meditation, especially long or intensive sittings, can bring up difficult experiences, so keep sessions short and stop if distress builds. People with a history of psychosis, bipolar disorder, severe trauma or a current crisis should talk to a clinician first; this is an untested idea.
modalities.tweet: For data lovers, a prototype practice: Thought Pattern Tally. Sit for 20 minutes, label each passing thought by type (planning, predicting, judging) and keep count. Over weeks you see which mental habits visit most, and that each visit passes on its own.

modalities.name: Prove-It Intervals
modalities.tagline: Hard intervals where 'I can't' thoughts get tested on the spot.
modalities.whatItIs: Prove-It Intervals is a new concept that brings the thought-testing of cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) into interval training. The predictable discomfort of short, hard bouts brings up thoughts like 'I can't' or 'this is too much', and the easy recovery minutes become a lab for comparing those thoughts with what you actually did.
modalities.coreIdea: Interval training produces the same self-doubting thoughts on cue, at a controlled intensity, which makes them unusually easy to catch and check in the moment. Each round asks the doubting voice to prove its claim, and the record of what you managed is evidence you can take into other hard moments.
modalities.whatYouDo: Twice a week, in a 30-minute session with a coach or class, you warm up and then do six rounds of one minute at a hard but sustainable effort, about 7 out of 10, on a bike or rowing machine, with two easy minutes between. Before each hard minute you rate how strongly you believe 'I can't keep this up', and in the easy minutes you note the thought that showed up and what actually happened. You finish with a cool-down and one written line on what the doubting voice got wrong.
modalities.whoItsFor: People whose self-doubt shows up as 'I can't' in many parts of life, and who like short, structured workouts with a clear measure of progress.
modalities.cautions: Hard bouts load the heart, so anyone with heart disease, chest pain, fainting or high blood pressure should get medical advice first, build up gradually and keep easy days between sessions. The aim is to test self-doubt, never to override real warning signs such as pain, dizziness or chest discomfort, which mean stop; the concept is untested.
modalities.tweet: Mid-burst in a hard workout, your mind says 'I can't'. Prove-It Intervals, a new concept: rate that thought before each burst, then compare it with what you did. A workout that doubles as a lab for anyone who talks themselves out of hard things.

modalities.name: Prediction Scrimmage
modalities.tagline: A friendly team game for testing fears about other people.
modalities.whatItIs: Prediction Scrimmage is a proposed group practice halfway between cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) and recreational team sport. Before a low-key, non-contact game, each player writes down one fear about how others will react, such as 'if I drop the disc, they will be annoyed', and the game becomes a live test of it.
modalities.coreIdea: Team games constantly produce the very moments that social fears are about, such as making a mistake, asking for the ball or disputing a call, but in a playful, low-stakes setting. Turning those moments into planned experiments, and comparing predictions with what happened in a circle afterwards, gives quick evidence from real people.
modalities.whatYouDo: Once a week for eight weeks, ten to fourteen people meet for 75 minutes with a coach who has CBT-informed training, warm up together and play small-sided games of a self-refereed, non-contact sport such as ultimate. Before play, each person writes one prediction and one action to try, like calling a foul calmly or asking for a pass, and after each game the group compares predictions with what actually happened. Results are tracked from week to week, so players can see how their predictions change.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who worry a lot about what others think, especially those who avoid groups but would rather learn by playing than by sitting in a room talking.
modalities.cautions: Running and jumping bring a risk of sprains and knocks to the head, so warm up, keep the game non-contact, stop playing after any head knock and check with a doctor first if you have heart or joint problems. Intense social fear or panic may need a therapist, and no one should be pushed into an experiment; the idea is untested.
modalities.tweet: Pitch for a new game: Prediction Scrimmage. Before a friendly match, write down one fear about other people, like 'if I drop it, they'll be annoyed'. Play, then compare notes. Real evidence from real teammates, for anyone who worries what others think.

modalities.name: Worry, Run, Reread
modalities.tagline: Rate a worry, go for a steady run, then rate it again.
modalities.whatItIs: Worry, Run, Reread is a new concept that pairs the thought ratings of cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) with steady endurance exercise such as jogging or brisk walking. You write down a worry and rate how true it feels before a run, then look at it again afterwards and write a fresh view, so each run becomes a small experiment in how much a thought's grip depends on your state.
modalities.coreIdea: Thoughts often feel most convincing when you are tense, tired or stuck indoors, and a steady bout of exercise can change how they look. Logging the same worry before and after, week after week, builds personal evidence that how strongly a thought grips you is not the same as how true it is.
modalities.whatYouDo: Three times a week, alone or with a running buddy, you write one current worry and rate how true it feels from 0 to 100, then jog or walk briskly for about 30 minutes at a pace where you could still talk. When you get back you read the worry again, re-rate it and write one alternative view that now seems possible. At the end of each week you look over the ratings, and a coach or CBT practitioner can help you set up the routine in the first few sessions.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who ruminate, who notice their thinking clears when they move, and who like routines and numbers they can track.
modalities.cautions: Running injuries are common, so build up time and distance gradually, take rest days and get medical advice first if you have heart disease or another medical condition. Exercise that becomes compulsive deserves professional attention, and this untested idea is no replacement for care if worry or low mood persists.
modalities.tweet: Worry, Run, Reread: an experimental routine for worriers. Write down a worry and rate how true it feels, go for a steady 30-minute jog, then read it again. Week by week you collect your own evidence that a thought's grip is not the same as its truth.

modalities.name: Counterweight Log
modalities.tagline: A strength training log that doubles as evidence against self-doubt.
modalities.whatItIs: Counterweight Log is a proposed practice that pairs a simple, progressive strength program with the evidence logs of cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT). Alongside your sets and weights, you track one harsh belief about yourself, such as 'I never stick with anything', and the slowly growing record of what you lifted becomes evidence to weigh against it.
modalities.coreIdea: Strength training gives unusually clear, written proof that effort adds up over weeks and months, and CBT asks you to collect evidence against unhelpful beliefs about who you are. Keeping both in one log turns each session into a small counterweight to a belief that may have gone unchallenged for years.
modalities.whatYouDo: Twice a week you do a short, set program of squats, presses, rows, hip hinges and carries at moderate loads, guided by a coach for the first few weeks. Before each session you rate one belief from 0 to 100, and afterwards you write down the sets you did and one fact from your week that does not fit the belief. Every four weeks you review the log with your coach or therapist, re-rate the belief and decide whether to add a little weight.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who doubt they can follow through or get better at anything, and who respond well to clear numbers and steady, visible progress.
modalities.cautions: Learn good technique, add weight slowly and breathe out on the effort rather than holding your breath, and get medical advice first if you have high blood pressure, heart problems or serious eye disease. If the focus drifts to body size or appearance, or low mood persists, talk to a professional, since this untested idea is no substitute for care.
modalities.tweet: Your workout log could double as evidence against self-doubt. That's the idea behind the Counterweight Log: track one harsh belief, like 'I never stick with anything', in the same notebook as your strength sessions, and watch the record grow against it.

modalities.name: Trick by Trick
modalities.tagline: Teach a dog a trick in small rewarded steps, then teach yourself.
modalities.whatItIs: Trick by Trick is a new concept for therapist-led sessions halfway between cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) and animal-assisted therapy. With a handler's guidance, you teach a willing, trained dog a simple new behavior in tiny, rewarded steps, then apply the same approach to a goal of your own that has felt too big to start.
modalities.coreIdea: Watching an animal learn makes the logic of behavior change visible: break it down, reward small wins and never punish slow progress. Offering that patience to an animal first may make it easier to offer it to your own stuck goals.
modalities.whatYouDo: In weekly 50-minute sessions for about eight weeks, a licensed therapist and a certified dog-and-handler team meet you in a quiet room or garden. For the first half you teach the dog one small behavior with food rewards and gentle timing, guided by the handler; for the second half you and the therapist break one of your own goals into equally small steps and plan a reward for each. The next week you review both the dog's progress and yours.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who are stuck on a goal and hard on themselves about it, such as getting back into a routine after a spell of low mood, and who enjoy animals and learn best hands-on.
modalities.cautions: Allergies, fear of dogs and bites are real risks, so contact is optional and supervised, hygiene rules apply, and the handler ends the session whenever the dog shows signs of stress or tiredness. For depression or anxiety, look for a licensed professional who offers this kind of work alongside other care; the concept itself is untested.
modalities.tweet: Teaching a dog a trick takes small steps, quick rewards and zero scolding. Trick by Trick, an untested idea: do just that with a therapist and a trained dog, then use the same steps on your own stuck goal. For anyone harder on themselves than on a puppy.

modalities.name: Four Corners Form
modalities.tagline: Four slow movements, each checking one part of the stress cycle.
modalities.whatItIs: Four Corners Form is a proposed movement routine halfway between cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) and qigong. It pairs four slow, breath-paced movements with the four corners of the CBT cycle (body, feelings, thoughts and actions), so one short routine walks you through checking and adjusting each in turn.
modalities.coreIdea: CBT teaches that body sensations, feelings, thoughts and actions keep feeding each other, and qigong trains a calm, focused mind through slow, repeated movement. Giving each corner of that cycle its own movement turns a mental checklist into a calm routine the body remembers.
modalities.whatYouDo: You learn the routine in a six-week class with an instructor, then practice it alone for about 15 minutes a day, standing or seated. Each of the four movements carries one question: where is the tension, what is my mood from 0 to 10, what is my mind saying and is it fair, and what is one small helpful thing I could do next. You repeat the round three times, letting the breath slow, and end by writing down the action you chose.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who like the logic of CBT but forget to use it when stressed, and people who want a gentle, structured routine that settles the body while organizing the mind.
modalities.cautions: The movements are gentle, but adapt them to your body and sit if standing is tiring, and anyone with a history of psychosis or another serious mental illness should get medical advice before starting qigong-style practice. It is an untested self-help idea, so keep up any care you already have and get professional help if distress persists.
modalities.tweet: Four slow movements, four questions: where is the tension, how is my mood, what is my mind saying, what is one helpful next step? Four Corners Form is a new qigong-style routine for people who forget their coping skills the moment stress hits.

modalities.name: The Follow-Up Club
modalities.tagline: Turn acquaintances into friends with small, tracked follow-ups.
modalities.whatItIs: The Follow-Up Club is a new concept for a small weekly group halfway between cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) and intentional socializing. Members each choose someone they would like to know better, plan one small follow-up such as a message or an invitation, and work on the thoughts that usually stop them from sending it.
modalities.coreIdea: Many friendships stall not at the first meeting but at the follow-up, often because of quick predictions like 'they are too busy for me' or 'I will seem needy'. Planning the step, writing down the prediction and reporting back the next week turns reaching out into a repeatable habit that gathers its own evidence.
modalities.whatYouDo: Six to ten people meet for an hour each week, in person or online, with a volunteer host trained to use a simple CBT worksheet. Each member names one person and one next step, writes down the thought that makes it hard along with a more balanced view, and commits to a time to do it. The following week everyone reports what happened, compares it with their prediction and picks the next step.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who feel lonely after a move, a breakup, retirement or a new job, and anyone who meets people easily enough but rarely turns those meetings into friendships.
modalities.cautions: Favor people who feel safe and step back from anyone hostile or controlling, since the goal is good connection, not more contact at any cost. If social situations bring intense fear, panic or avoidance, or low mood persists, talk to a doctor or therapist, as this untested idea is no substitute for care.
modalities.tweet: Lonely, but full of acquaintances? The Follow-Up Club is a new idea: a small weekly group where you pick one person, plan one message or invite, note the fear that stops you, and report back next week. Friendship as a habit you practice together.

modalities.name: Waymarker Walks
modalities.tagline: One problem-solving step at each landmark, open noticing in between.
modalities.whatItIs: Waymarker Walks is a proposed practice halfway between the structured problem-solving of cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) and nature walks. On a loop through a park or countryside, you pick five landmarks along the way, take one step of problem-solving at each, and spend the stretches in between simply noticing the landscape.
modalities.coreIdea: Structured problem-solving works best in clear steps, but a tired, worried mind tends to rush or go round in circles, and natural settings are thought to let effortful attention recover. Spacing the steps out with stretches of open noticing gives each step a fresher mind, so the plan you reach at the end comes from a clearer head.
modalities.whatYouDo: You walk a 45 to 60 minute loop with a friend or walking coach, or alone with a notebook, and choose five landmarks along the route, such as a gate, a bridge or a big tree. At the first you name one current problem, at the second you list options, at the third you weigh their pros and cons, at the fourth you choose one, and at the fifth you plan the first small step and when you will take it. Between landmarks you put the problem down and notice sights, sounds and smells, so each step starts fresh.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who go round in circles with a decision or worry, and who think better side by side and on the move than face to face across a table.
modalities.cautions: Plan the route, check the weather, carry water and tell someone where you are going, since slips, heat, cold and getting lost are real outdoor risks. This untested idea can support everyday decisions, but persistent worry or low mood calls for a doctor or therapist.
modalities.tweet: Stuck on a decision? Waymarker Walks, a new concept: pick five landmarks on a loop and take one problem-solving step at each (name it, list options, weigh, choose, plan). In between, just notice the trees and sky. For people who think better outdoors.

modalities.name: Eyewitness Pause
modalities.tagline: Check an alarming thought against what your senses actually report.
modalities.whatItIs: Eyewitness Pause is a new concept halfway between the evidence-checking of cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) and sensory mindfulness. When an alarming thought tells you something about the present, such as 'everyone is staring' or 'something is wrong', you pause and gather plain sensory evidence like a careful eyewitness, then compare it with what the thought claimed.
modalities.coreIdea: CBT weighs thoughts against evidence, and sensory mindfulness offers the most direct evidence there is: what you can see, hear and feel right now. Separating the raw report of the senses from the story laid on top of it shows which parts of an alarming thought the moment actually supports.
modalities.whatYouDo: You learn the steps from a short course or workbook and practice daily for 15 minutes, then use a three-minute version in the moment. When a thought alarms you, you write it in a note, then spend about a minute each listing only what you can see, hear and feel in your body, with no interpretation, as an eyewitness would. Then you read the thought again and mark which parts the senses support, which they do not, and what you would like to do next.
modalities.whoItsFor: People whose anxious thoughts make confident claims about what is happening around them, and who want a quick, structured way back to the facts of the moment.
modalities.cautions: It is a gentle self-help idea, untested as a combination and not a stand-alone answer to panic disorder, PTSD or psychosis, which call for a qualified therapist. Some people notice heightened sensitivity to sights and sounds, or difficult memories, during sensory practice, so start gently and stop if it feels like too much.
modalities.tweet: When a thought says 'everyone is staring', be an eyewitness instead. Eyewitness Pause, an untested idea: for three minutes, note only what you see, hear and feel, then check which parts of the thought the moment supports. For minds that jump to conclusions.

modalities.name: The Answer Song
modalities.tagline: Turn a harsh recurring thought into a chorus, then write the reply.
modalities.whatItIs: The Answer Song is a proposed songwriting practice halfway between cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) and music. You take a harsh thought that keeps coming back, set it to a simple tune as a chorus, and then write verses that answer it with evidence and a fairer view, the way an answer song replies to an earlier hit.
modalities.coreIdea: Putting an automatic thought into a chorus makes it easier to hear as a repeated tune rather than the truth, and a balanced reply set to music is easier to remember than a line on a worksheet. The finished song becomes a portable, catchy version of thought work.
modalities.whatYouDo: Over six weekly sessions, one to one or in a small group led by a music therapist or songwriting coach with CBT training, you pick one thought, such as 'I always mess things up', and set it to a simple tune, with no musical skill needed. Each week you add a verse that weighs the evidence, recalls times the thought was wrong or offers a kinder, realistic view, and you record the song on a phone. Between sessions you listen back and notice which lines feel truest.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who find worksheets dry but love music, and people whose harsh inner voice already sounds like a song stuck on repeat.
modalities.cautions: Music can stir strong feelings, and for people prone to rumination, dwelling on a sad tune can deepen low mood, so notice how the song leaves you and keep the volume moderate. Clinical work calls for a credentialed music therapist, and this untested idea is an add-on to professional care for serious depression, not a replacement.
modalities.tweet: Songwriters answer old hits all the time. The Answer Song is a new concept that does it for your inner critic: turn a harsh thought like 'I always mess things up' into a chorus, then write verses that answer it with evidence. No musical skill needed.

modalities.name: Two Loyalties Dialogue
modalities.tagline: Honor what your stuck pattern is loyal to, then choose your values.
modalities.whatItIs: Two Loyalties Dialogue is a new concept for therapy halfway between acceptance and commitment therapy (ACT) and Coherence Therapy. It sees a stuck pattern as loyal to an old emotional purpose, such as staying small so as not to outshine a parent, and sets that loyalty side by side with what you value today, so you can make room for both and choose consciously.
modalities.coreIdea: Coherence Therapy holds that a symptom makes emotional sense, and ACT asks you to make room for inner experience while acting on your values. Naming the old loyalty with respect instead of fighting it, and setting it beside a value you live by now, may let the choice between them become truly your own.
modalities.whatYouDo: Over 8 to 12 weekly sessions with a licensed therapist, you pick one stuck pattern and, through gentle sentence completion and imagery, find what it has been loyal to, for example 'if I succeed, I leave my family behind'. You then name the value it competes with and, in session, hold both in mind at once without forcing either to win. Each week you choose one small value-based action and notice how the old loyalty responds.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who know what matters to them yet keep acting against it, and who want to understand why before pushing harder.
modalities.cautions: Feeling an old loyalty fully can be intense, so this belongs with a licensed clinician experienced in trauma, especially for anyone with severe trauma, dissociation or a current crisis, and medical causes of a symptom should be checked first. It is an untested combination, not a replacement for well-tested care for conditions such as major depression or PTSD.
modalities.tweet: Some stuck habits stay loyal to something old, like not outshining your family. Two Loyalties Dialogue, a new therapy concept: name that loyalty with respect, hold it beside what you value now, then choose. For anyone who keeps acting against their values.

modalities.name: Shake and Stand
modalities.tagline: Let gentle tremors come and go, then stand and take one step.
modalities.whatItIs: Shake and Stand is a proposed body practice halfway between acceptance and commitment therapy (ACT) and tension and trauma releasing exercises (TRE), in which the legs start to tremble on their own after tiring stretches. You practice the ACT skill of willingness, making room for what you cannot fully control, by letting gentle tremors come and go, then stand up and take one small step toward something you value.
modalities.coreIdea: A tremor you can allow but not fully steer is a bodily stand-in for the feelings and thoughts we fight against, and noticing the mind's urge to stop or analyze it is practice in letting experience be. Standing up afterwards and naming one value-based action links that willingness directly to living by what matters.
modalities.whatYouDo: After learning the exercises with a certified provider, you practice at home for about 30 minutes: ten minutes of gentle leg-tiring stretches, then up to ten minutes lying on your back with bent knees, letting mild tremors run. When thoughts like 'this is weird' or 'make it stop' appear, you name them as thoughts and let the shaking continue only as long as it feels comfortable, stopping any time by straightening your legs. Then you stand, take a slow breath and say aloud one small action you will take today that matters to you.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who carry tension and find themselves fighting their own feelings, and who would rather practice acceptance through the body than through talking.
modalities.cautions: Tremor work can stir strong emotions or memories, so anyone with severe trauma, dissociation, psychosis, bipolar disorder or another serious condition should learn it only with a clinically trained provider and alongside their own care. Ask a doctor first if you have epilepsy, are pregnant or are recovering from surgery or injury, and stop if you feel overwhelmed, in pain or panicky; the idea is untested.
modalities.tweet: Acceptance, practiced through the body: Shake and Stand, a new idea. Tire your legs with gentle stretches, lie down and let the natural tremor come and go, then stand and name one thing you'll do today that matters. For people who fight their own feelings.

modalities.name: The Felt Compass
modalities.tagline: Sense what matters in the body, then take one next step.
modalities.whatItIs: The Felt Compass is a new concept halfway between acceptance and commitment therapy (ACT) and Focusing. Instead of choosing values from a list, you let a felt sense, the vague bodily sense of what a situation means to you, form around the question 'what matters to me here?', find words that fit it, and turn them into one next step.
modalities.coreIdea: Values picked from a list can feel like shoulds, while a value found through the body tends to carry its own pull. Checking the words against the felt sense until they fit gives you a value you have actually sensed, and one small committed step keeps it from staying an idea.
modalities.whatYouDo: With a listening partner or a Focusing-trained coach, you sit for 30 to 45 minutes, eyes closed, and bring to mind a situation where you feel torn or stuck. You let a felt sense of what matters in it form and try out words or images until one fits, while your partner simply reflects back what you say. You end by naming one small action that follows from it, which you check in on next time.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who feel unsure what they truly want, or whose values sound right on paper but do not move them, and who like a quiet, body-aware way of exploring.
modalities.cautions: Usually gentle, but turning attention inward can bring up strong feelings or painful memories, and some people find the felt sense hard to notice at first. People with severe trauma, dissociation, psychosis or a current crisis should work with a qualified therapist, as this is an untested idea.
modalities.tweet: Can't tell what you really want? The Felt Compass is a new concept: sit with a listener, let a sense of what matters form in your body, find words that fit, then take one small step. Values you feel, not values picked off a list.
